dependence.note: Section 5.2 evaluates 6 LLMs as few-shot classifiers of nanoparticle shape; the headline LLM result (GPT-4 0.81 average accuracy beating Random Forest 0.80, Table 4) is entirely LLM output. GPT-3.5 was also used auxiliarily to paraphrase the synthesis-text templates (frozen in the repo).

claim.statement: With 8 in-context examples drawn only from the target class and syntheses presented as text, GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) predicts calcium-carbonate nanoparticle shapes with 0.81 +/- 0.07 average accuracy (Cube 0.71, Stick 0.68, Sphere 0.88, Flat 0.90, Amorphous 0.87), exceeding the best classical model (Random Forest 0.80), whereas 'GPT-4-turbo' (gpt-4-0125-preview) reaches only 0.69 +/- 0.11 with a collapse on spheres (0.44) (Table 4; Section 5.2.3).
claim.metric: Per-shape accuracy of presence/absence prediction on a held-out test subset (balanced per shape), mean +/- SD over 5 repeated random draws of the in-context examples; average over the 5 shapes.
claim.original_source: Paper Table 4 (also reproduced verbatim in the repo README) and Table 2; Table 8 gives GPT-4 accuracy vs N examples and test-subset size; results_llm.xlsx in the repo

messages.content: You are an expert in the synthesis of nanomaterials. You analyze the conditions for obtaining a nanomaterial and predict what particle shapes will be present in the synthesized material. There are five particle shapes: 'Cube', 'Stick', 'Sphere', 'Flat' and 'Amorphous'. A nanomaterial can contain particles of different shapes. If you cannot say exactly what it is, list the forms that have the highest probability in those conditions.
<'Cube, Stick' etc.>  (x N=8, all from the target class: 'strict' sampler)

params.test_subset_size: 0.15 / 0.20 / 0.33 explored (Table 8); Table 4 configuration not stated explicitly

protocol.evaluation: Automatic: parse the shape list in the reply; per-shape binary accuracy vs the labelled shape set; average over shapes; mean +/- SD over 5 repeats.

domain_notes: The dataset is 215 calcium-carbonate co-precipitation syntheses with SEM-derived shape labels (cube/stick/sphere/flat/amorphous, multi-label). The few-shot 'strict' sampler puts only same-class examples in the prompt, so the reported accuracies partly measure the model's tendency to copy the demonstrated label ('confirmation experiment' framing in Section 5.2.2) rather than genuine synthesis-to-morphology reasoning. Sphere accuracy of GPT-4-turbo (0.44) vs GPT-4 (0.88) with identical prompts illustrates large between-snapshot variance in this setting.
